### cylinder3d {#sec-example-laminar-cylinder3d}

This example examines a steady flow past a cylinder placed in a channel.
The cylinder is offset somewhat from the center of the flow to make the steady-state symmetrical flow unstable.
At the inlet, a Poiseuille profile is imposed on the velocity, whereas the outlet implements a Dirichlet pressure condition set by $p = 0$, inspired by [@turek:96].
For high resolution, low `latticeU`, and enough time to converge, the results for pressure drop, drag, and lift lie within the estimated intervals for the exact results.
An unsteady flow with Kármán vortex street can be created by changing the Reynolds number to $Re=100$.
This 3D version of [[`laminar/cylinder2d`](/examples/laminar/cylinder2d/cylinder2d.qmd)]{.content-visible when-format="html"}[`laminar/cylinder2d` (@sec-example-laminar-cylinder2d)]{.content-visible when-format="pdf"} also shows the usage of the STL-reader.

#### Governing equations

The domain $\Omega \times \I$, the channel $[0, 2.5] \times [0, 0.41] \times [0, 0.41]$ without the cylinder times $\R_{\geq 0}$, is considered with the following governing equations with the velocity field $\vel \in \R^3$ and the pressure $p \in \R$ for the incompressible flow of a Newtonian fluid with kinematic viscosity $\nu \in \R_{> 0}$ and constant density $\rho \in \R_{> 0}$,
\begin{align}
    \nabla \cdot \vel &= 0 \quad \text{in} \quad \Omega \times \I, \\
    \partial_t \vel + (\vel \cdot \nabla) \vel &= -\frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p + \nu \Delta \vel \quad \text{in} \quad \Omega \times \I.
\end{align}

#### Boundary conditions

The boundary $\partial \Omega = \Gamma_D \cup \Gamma_\text{out} \cup \Gamma_{\mathrm{no\text{-}slip}}$ consists of the inlet $\Gamma_D$ at $x = 0$ (MN 3), the outlet $\Gamma_\text{out}$ at $x = 2.5\,\mathrm{m}$ (MN 4), and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{no\text{-}slip}}$, the four channel walls (MN 2) and the surface of the cylinder (MN 5),
\begin{align}
    \vel &= (u_\text{in}(y, z, t), 0, 0)^\top \quad \text{on} \quad \Gamma_D \times \I, \\
    p &= 0 \quad \text{on} \quad \Gamma_\text{out} \times \I, \\
    \vel &= \mathbf{0} \quad \text{on} \quad \Gamma_{\mathrm{no\text{-}slip}} \times \I.
\end{align}
The inflow profile is the product of two parabolas across the square cross section,
$$
    u_\text{in}(y, z, t) = s(t)\, \frac{16\, U_\text{max}\, y z (H - y)(H - z)}{H^4}, \qquad U_\text{max} = \tfrac{9}{4} U,
$$
whose mean velocity is $U$ once it is fully developed.
`setTemporalValues()` raises it from rest with a polynomial ramp $s(t)$ during the first $40\,\%$ of the simulated time, updated every $0.03\,\mathrm{s}$.
The fluid is initially at rest.

#### Domain

The geometry is read from `cylinder3d.stl` (@fig-cylinder3d-geometry), which is given in millimetres and scaled by $0.001$: a channel of length $2.5\,\mathrm{m}$ with the square cross section $H \times H$, $H = 0.41\,\mathrm{m}$, and a cylinder of diameter $D = 0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ that spans the whole height of the channel, with its axis at $(x, y) = (0.5\,\mathrm{m}, 0.2\,\mathrm{m})$, slightly below the centre line.
This is the setup of the test case 3D-1Z of @turek:96.
With the mean inflow velocity $U = 0.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $\nu = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, the Reynolds number is $Re = U D / \nu = 20$, and the flow becomes steady.
The FreeCAD model `cylinder3d.fcstd` the STL file was created from is part of the example.

`prepareGeometry()` marks the cells inside the STL surface as fluid (MN 1) and a layer of one cell around it as wall (MN 2).
It then marks the wall cells at the inlet and the outlet end as MN 3 and MN 4, and the remaining wall cells inside the channel, those of the cylinder, as MN 5.

![Geometry of `cylinder3d`, the surface of `cylinder3d.stl`: the channel and the cylinder spanning its height.](/examples/laminar/cylinder3d/doc/fig/cylinder3dGeometry.png){width="70%" #fig-cylinder3d-geometry .lightbox}

#### Discretization \& Descriptor
In this example, the domain is discretized with a uniform grid with the lattice spacing $\Delta x = D / N$, where $N = 10$ cells resolve the diameter of the cylinder, which gives about $417\,000$ fluid cells.
The mesh is split into $7$ cuboids, or into one cuboid per process with MPI.

The LBM collision operator is the BGK operator with a single relaxation time ([Collision Operators](/content/02_core.qmd#collision-operators)), used as `BGKdynamics`, together with the D3Q19 velocity set ([Lattice Structures](/content/01_introduction.qmd#sec-lattice-structures)). The lattice uses single precision.
The channel walls (MN 2) are treated with `BounceBack`, the inlet (MN 3) with `InterpolatedVelocity`, the outlet (MN 4) with `InterpolatedPressure`, and the cylinder (MN 5) with the Bouzidi boundary, `setBouzidiBoundary()`, which takes the exact position of the STL surface between the lattice nodes into account ([Define Boundary Method](/content/06_initial_boundary.qmd#sec-defineBoundaryMethod)). Without the `BOUZIDI` define in `case.h`, the cylinder falls back to `BounceBack`.

The corresponding lattice is defined inside the case definition in `case.h` as in @lst-cylinder3d-case.

::: {#lst-cylinder3d-case}
```{.cpp}
using MyCase = Case<
  NavierStokes, Lattice<float, descriptors::D3Q19<>>
>;
```
Case definition for the `cylinder3d` example.
:::

The unit converter `UnitConverterFromResolutionAndRelaxationTime` derives the time step size from the resolution and the lattice relaxation time.
The parameters are given in @tbl-cylinder3d-params.

| Parameter | Symbol | Value | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RESOLUTION` | $N$ | $10$ | cells per cylinder diameter $D$ |
| `REYNOLDS` | $Re$ | $20$ | Reynolds number $U D / \nu$, which sets $\nu = 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$ |
| `PHYS_MAX_T` | $T$ | $16\,\mathrm{s}$ | simulated time, $16\,000$ time steps |
| `PHYS_CHAR_VELOCITY` | $U$ | $0.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ | mean velocity of the fully developed inflow |
| `LATTICE_RELAXATION_TIME` | $\tau$ | $0.53$ | lattice relaxation time |
| `PHYS_CHAR_DENSITY` | $\rho$ | $1\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ | density |
| `RADIUS_CYLINDER` | $D/2$ | $0.05\,\mathrm{m}$ | radius of the cylinder |
| `PHYS_VTK_ITER_T` | | $0.3\,\mathrm{s}$ | interval of the VTK output, the heat maps and the drag plot |
| `PHYS_STAT_ITER_T` | | $0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ | interval of the console statistics and the drag evaluation |
| `RAMP_UP_UPDATE` | | $0.03\,\mathrm{s}$ | interval at which the inflow is updated during the ramp-up |
| `RAMP_UP_END_FRACTION` | | $0.4$ | fraction of $T$ after which the inflow is fully developed |
| `VTK_ENABLED` | | `true` | write VTK output and heat maps |
| `GNUPLOT_ENABLED` | | `true` | write the drag over time |

: Parameters of `cylinder3d`, as set in `main()`. {#tbl-cylinder3d-params}

#### Validation

The velocity, the pressure and a refinement quality criterion based on the Knudsen number are written every $0.3\,\mathrm{s}$, together with heat maps of the velocity and of the quality criterion in the plane $z = H/2$.
@fig-cylinder3d-velocity shows the velocity magnitude in this plane at the end of the simulation.

![Magnitude of the physical velocity of `cylinder3d` in the plane $z = H/2$ at $t = 15.9\,\mathrm{s}$, visualized in ParaView.](/examples/laminar/cylinder3d/doc/fig/cylinder3d_velocity.png){width="100%" #fig-cylinder3d-velocity .lightbox}

The heat maps are produced without ParaView, directly in `getResults()` (@lst-cylinder3d-heatmap).
`SuperEuklidNorm3D` computes the magnitude $|\vel|$ of the physical velocity, and `BlockReduction3D2D` samples this 3D functor on the plane with the normal $(0, 0, 1)$ through the centre of the mesh, the plane $z = H/2$.

::: {#lst-cylinder3d-heatmap}
```{.cpp}
SuperEuklidNorm3D<T> normVel(velocity);
BlockReduction3D2D<T> planeReduction(normVel, Vector<T,3>{0, 0, 1});
// write output as JPEG
heatmap::write(planeReduction, iT);
```
Reduction of the velocity magnitude to the plane $z = H/2$ and output as a heat map in `getResults()`.
:::

@fig-cylinder3d-heatmap shows these heat maps during the ramp-up of the inflow and at the end of the simulation.
As long as the inflow is weak, the fluid flows around the cylinder almost symmetrically in $x$. With the growing velocity, the region of low velocity behind the cylinder stretches into a wake, and the flow accelerates through the gaps between the cylinder and the channel walls.
After the ramp-up, the velocity field hardly changes any more.

::: {.image-slider .image-slider-wide}
::: {#fig-cylinder3d-heatmap layout-ncol="3"}

![$t = 15.9\,\mathrm{s}$, end of the simulation](/examples/laminar/cylinder3d/doc/fig/heatmap/velocity_iT0015900.jpeg)

Heat maps of the velocity magnitude $|\vel|$ in m/s of `cylinder3d` in the plane $z = H/2$, written by `heatmap::write()` from the `BlockReduction3D2D` of `SuperEuklidNorm3D`. For this page, the colour range is fixed to $[0, 0.6]\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for all time steps, so that they are comparable. `getResults()` itself does not fix it, so the heat maps it writes are scaled to the maximum of each time step.
:::
:::

Every $0.1\,\mathrm{s}$, `getResults()` evaluates the drag coefficient of the cylinder, $c_D = 2 F_D / (\rho U^2 D H)$ with the drag force $F_D$, and writes it over time to `tmp/gnuplotData/`. It also computes the pressure drop across the cylinder, but does not output it.
@fig-cylinder3d-drag compares the drag coefficient with the interval $6.05 \le c_D \le 6.25$ that @turek:96 give for the test case 3D-1Z.
During the ramp-up, the drag follows the stepwise updates of the inflow. Afterwards it settles at $c_D = 6.31$ at the end of the simulation, about $1\,\%$ above the reference interval with the coarse default resolution of $N = 10$.
The drag plot that the example writes itself shows the 2D reference value $5.58$ of the test case 2D-1 instead.

![Drag coefficient $c_D$ of `cylinder3d` over time with $N = 10$, compared with the reference interval of the test case 3D-1Z. The drag rises while the inflow is ramped up during the first $6.4\,\mathrm{s}$ and then settles.](/examples/laminar/cylinder3d/doc/fig/drag/drag.svg){width="80%" #fig-cylinder3d-drag .lightbox}

#### Files

```
cylinder3d/
├── cylinder3d.cpp     main(): parameters, then mesh, geometry, lattice, initial values and time loop
├── case.h             Case type, geometry from the STL file, boundary conditions, inflow ramp-up, drag and output
├── cylinder3d.stl     geometry of the channel and the cylinder, in millimetres
├── cylinder3d.fcstd   FreeCAD model of the geometry
└── Makefile
```

`case.h` reads the geometry from `cylinder3d.stl`, a path relative to the directory the example is run from, which therefore has to be the example's own directory.
The results are written to `tmp/` there: `vtkData/cylinder3d.pvd` opens all time steps in ParaView, `imageData/` holds the heat maps and `gnuplotData/` the drag over time. The heat maps and plots are drawn with gnuplot; without it, only the data in `gnuplotData/data/` is written.
